title: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
intro: Post-traumatic stress disorder can develop after experiencing or witnessing a terrifying event such as violence, an accident, war, disaster or abuse. People relive the event, avoid reminders and feel constantly on edge. PTSD is a real and treatable condition, and trauma-focused psychotherapy is highly effective.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: PTSD involves intrusive memories, flashbacks and nightmares, avoidance of people, places or thoughts that remind of the event, negative changes in mood and beliefs such as guilt, numbness or detachment, and heightened arousal with sleep problems, irritability, jumpiness and poor concentration. Symptoms last longer than a month and cause distress or impairment.

sections.heading: Who is affected
paragraphs: Most people feel shaken after trauma and recover over weeks. A minority develop PTSD. Risk is higher after repeated or intense trauma, in childhood, with lack of support, previous mental illness or stressful life circumstances. Refugees, survivors of violence and emergency workers are at higher risk. Depression, anxiety, substance use and physical complaints often occur alongside PTSD.

sections.heading: Getting help
paragraphs: See a doctor or psychotherapist if symptoms persist beyond a few weeks or interfere with life. Diagnosis is based on a careful conversation. It can help to bring a trusted person, and you do not need to describe all details at first. Interpreters can be requested when language is a barrier.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing are recommended first. They help process memories safely and change unhelpful beliefs. Antidepressants may help some people, particularly when therapy is not available or in the presence of depression. Sleeping tablets should be used with care. Treatment of substance use and ongoing safety issues is also important.

sections.heading: Self-help and support
paragraphs: Regular routines, exercise, sleep, contact with supportive people and avoiding alcohol and drugs help. Grounding techniques, such as noticing five things you see or hear, can ease flashbacks. Do not force yourself to relive events alone. Support groups, victim services and community organisations provide additional help. In a crisis, contact emergency services or a crisis line.

examples.title: Using a grounding exercise
examples.text: Imagine a loud noise triggers a flashback. You could look around and name five things you see, feel your feet on the floor and breathe slowly until you feel anchored in the present.

examples.title: Seeking therapy
examples.text: Suppose you hesitate to talk about your experience. You might tell the therapist at the outset what you are ready to share and ask how therapy is paced.
